title: As the Worm Turns
subtitle: The first Internet worms of 2005
description: How a never-disclosed Windows vulnerability was quickly reverse-engineered from the patch that fixed it and turned into more than 12 potent and damaging Internet worms in three days. What does this mean for the future of Internet security?

beats.t: Hi, I'm Leo Laporte, and this is something new for the TWiT lineup: Security Now! with Steve Gibson. Episode 1, recorded August 18, 2005.

You know Steve from This Week in Tech, The Screen Savers and Call for Help. Most people know him for SpinRite, the hard-drive recovery tool that inspired Norton Disk Doctor and still runs rings around it.
He first got my attention with the Iomega Zip drive "Click of Death." Steve, was it you who got Iomega to admit there was a problem?
I think it was really our show. We had someone from Iomega on the phone during The Screen Savers, and we got him to say on the air that Iomega would replace any drive with the Click of Death.
I made a WAV file of that clip and put it on my site. People emailed it to Iomega: "Here's what you said. I want a new drive."
And it worked!

beats.title: The Click of Death
beats.t: A failure in Iomega Zip drives that made a clicking sound and could damage disks. Steve's research and that recorded on-air promise helped owners get their drives replaced.
Before we get to the news, a bit about Steve. You found the first spyware, came up with the word "spyware," and wrote the first anti-spyware program.
I found it on my own machine. The Aureate adware was phoning home. Dale Haag publicized it, maybe a little too much. I wrote OptOut in a few days to remove it.
Then there's ShieldsUP!, your free online port scanner. How many systems has it tested now, 30 million?
39 million.
You've also called out Windows flaws: UnPlug n' Pray for the Universal Plug and Play problem, and DCOMbobulator for the DCOM flaw.
And you were nearly the only one warning about raw sockets in Windows. People called you hysterical. Then a few months ago Microsoft quietly turned raw sockets off.
Boy, did I take some heat for that one.

Then there's LeakTest. It's still our most downloaded freeware. Personal firewalls weren't checking whether a program really was the one you had allowed, so malware could pretend to be Internet Explorer and get out.

beats.title: Raw sockets
beats.t: Raw sockets let a program build its own network packets, including forged ones. That makes spoofed traffic and denial-of-service attacks easier. Steve criticized Microsoft for enabling them in Windows XP, and Microsoft later restricted them.
And after all that, you still use Windows!
Everybody else does. That puts me right in the middle of where the problem is.
That's the point of this show. Every week you'll take hard-to-follow security news and explain it so we can all understand it.

chapters.title: Zotob: Three Days from Patch to Worm

beats.t: Zotob is the "virus" that's been spreading around the world, especially through media companies.
Let's talk about Zotob, the "virus" that's been spreading around the world, especially through media companies.

On the 9th, Microsoft released its usual second-Tuesday-of-the-month patches. Within three days, attackers had studied one patch, worked out the flaw it fixed, and turned that into a worm aimed at Windows 2000.
Microsoft never actually described the vulnerability. Only the fix was public, and that was enough.

beats.title: Reverse-engineering a patch
beats.t: When a fix ships, attackers can compare the patched files with the old ones to see exactly what changed. That shows them where the hole is. Each patch is also a hint for unpatched machines.
Is that the fastest turnaround ever?
Yes. It's usually more like six weeks. The LSASS vulnerability came out in late April 2004, and the Sasser worm that used it took about six weeks to appear.

beats.title: What is LSASS?
beats.t: LSASS (Local Security Authority Subsystem Service, lsass.exe) is the core Windows process that checks passwords when you log in, enforces security policy and issues the access tokens that decide what each program may do. A flaw in LSASS hands an attacker the highest level of control over the machine.

beats.title: The LSASS flaw (MS04-011)
beats.t: On April 13, 2004, Microsoft patched a buffer overflow in LSASS (security bulletin MS04-011). Specially crafted network requests to the Windows file-sharing ports could overflow it and run the attacker's code, with no login needed. Windows 2000 and Windows XP were affected.

beats.title: The Sasser worm
beats.t: Sasser appeared on April 30, 2004, about 17 days after the patch. (On the show, Steve remembered it as about six weeks.) It scanned random Internet addresses on TCP port 445, used the LSASS flaw to get in, then copied itself to each new victim and kept scanning. No user action was needed.

beats.title: Sasser's impact
beats.t: Sasser often crashed LSASS, so infected PCs showed a shutdown countdown and rebooted over and over. It hit hundreds of thousands of machines, disrupting airline check-ins, newsrooms, hospitals and rail systems. Its author, an 18-year-old German student, was arrested in May 2004.
Why so fast? Are the attackers getting smarter, or was this one easy?
I think it's desperation. There hadn't been a usable new hole in 14 or 15 months, and they were still relying on the old LSASS flaw.
Their bot and worm tools are mature now. As soon as they had a new way to take control of Windows remotely, they added that code to their existing tools and released it.
So everything's ready to go. They just need a hole.

beats.title: By the numbers
beats.t: More than 12 different worm variants based on this one flaw appeared within three days of Microsoft's patch.
What are these guys after? And is it really a virus?
A lot of news stories called it a virus, but these are worms. A worm spreads by itself. A virus traditionally needs the user to do something to get infected.
Like opening an email attachment. So with this one, you don't have to click anything.

beats.title: Worm vs. virus
beats.t: Virus: needs help from the user, for example opening an infected attachment. Worm: spreads across the network on its own by exploiting a vulnerable service, with no clicks needed.
Right. The ideal target is a Windows 2000 machine. XP has the same vulnerability, and the patch fixes it there too, even on a fully updated XP Service Pack 2 system.

But XP, especially with Service Pack 1 and 2, has extra protections around anonymous and admin log-ons that block the attack. On Windows 2000, just an anonymous connection is enough to infect the machine.
XP Service Pack 2 also turns the Windows Firewall on by default, which blocks it as well.
So with any firewall, a router or software firewall, you're safe. The ones at risk are unpatched Windows 2000 machines with no firewall in front of them.
True. And most home users skipped from Windows 98 straight to XP. Windows 2000 is mostly a business system.
So how did Zotob get in? Even a home user on Windows 2000 with a direct broadband connection and no NAT router would have one more layer of protection.
The worm comes in through NetBIOS file-sharing ports 139 and 445, the same ports I built ShieldsUP! to warn people about about five years ago. Many ISPs now block them.

My cable provider, Cox, blocks them. I have a Windows 98 machine on my cable modem. When I drop my firewall and scan it with ShieldsUP!, ports 135 through 139 and 445 show up green, meaning stealthed by Cox.
More and more ISPs are doing that. In effect, they're putting a firewall in front of their customers.
Because they don't want customer machines turned into zombies that take remote commands and send spam.

beats.title: Ports 135–139 & 445
beats.t: These are the Windows networking and file-sharing ports (RPC, NetBIOS, SMB). Exposed directly to the Internet, they were the way in for Blaster, Sasser and Zotob. Many ISPs began blocking them by default.
So if ISPs block those ports, who got hit, and how?
CNN ran a big story Sunday night. ABC, the Financial Times, The New York Times, General Electric, UPS and even Caterpillar were infected. These are major corporations.
About 50% of corporate desktops still run Windows 2000 because it works. I use Windows 2000 myself. XP doesn't offer anything I need.
But those companies are behind firewalls. And they probably don't patch as fast as home users.

Exactly. The patch came out the Tuesday before the infections started. Windows 2000 can do automatic updates, but it doesn't push them as hard, and corporate machines usually have the feature turned off. It might not get through the corporate firewall anyway.
These companies were hit by Sasser and Blaster, so their perimeter firewalls are locked down tight. But some telecommuters' laptops got infected over the weekend while the worm was spreading...
...then on Monday they brought the laptops to work, plugged them into the network, and infected the company from inside.
So the people working from home brought it past the firewall into the trusted network, where there was no internal firewalling.

beats.title: The hard shell, soft center
beats.t: A perimeter firewall protects only the edge of the network. Once an infected laptop is plugged in inside, every unprotected machine on the internal network is exposed.
Is there a lesson here? Do people need to change how they do things?
I think so. If those Windows 2000 machines had their own personal firewalls, none of this would have happened. CNN and The New York Times were hit hard.
ZoneAlarm and Sygate have the technology for this. In fact, Symantec announced just yesterday that it's buying Sygate to get its corporate lockdown technology.
The idea is that every desktop runs a personal firewall, and IT controls its rules centrally. Nobody likes it because it gets in the way of using your computer, but it's clearly necessary.
Either that, or ban laptops!

Well, I have a friend at 3M whose company laptop can only reach the Internet through a VPN tunnel into 3M's network. He hates it because it's slower, but their IT people have it locked down so tightly that nothing else can run.
And now you know why they do that.
Now it's very clear that was a good policy.

beats.title: Takeaways
beats.t: 1) Patch quickly, because patches show attackers where the holes are. 2) Run a firewall on every machine, not just at the edge. 3) Treat laptops that come back from outside as untrusted. 4) Close or block the NetBIOS/SMB ports.
So is this something new, or just another network worm that found one unwatched hole?

It's another network worm. What matters is that it went after Windows 2000 and not XP. Between XP's internal policies and Service Pack 2's default firewall, nobody could have written this worm for XP.
We talked about this on Call for Help. Now that XP is getting locked down, attackers will have to look for other ways in.
Since that show, there have already been several remote take-over vulnerabilities in third-party software, especially backup software.
It's taken Microsoft about 15 years to lock this down, but its policies are finally showing real improvement. So attackers will move toward other vendors' software.
Steve Gibson, you did it again.
Always a pleasure, Leo.
That's Security Now! It comes out every Thursday at midnight, so you can download it for your Friday or weekend, on AOL Radio or our feed. Thanks to AOL Radio for the bandwidth. See you next time!

quiz.q: How long after Microsoft's patch did the first Zotob-family worms appear?
quiz.explain: Attackers reverse-engineered the patch and released worms within three days. Earlier worms took much longer; Sasser came about 17 days after its patch.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between a worm and a virus?
options: A worm spreads by itself; a virus needs the user to act
quiz.explain: A worm exploits a network service and spreads on its own. A virus traditionally needs a user action, such as opening an attachment.

quiz.q: What does LSASS, the Windows service attacked by the Sasser worm, do?
options: Checks logins and enforces Windows security policy
quiz.explain: LSASS (lsass.exe) handles logins, security policy and access tokens. The flaw patched in MS04-011 let Sasser take over the machine through port 445 with no user action.

quiz.q: Which Windows version was the worm's main target?
quiz.explain: On Windows 2000, an anonymous connection was enough to infect an unpatched machine. XP's log-on restrictions and SP2's default firewall blocked the attack.

quiz.q: Which ports did the worm use to get in?
quiz.explain: The NetBIOS file-sharing ports 139 and 445, the same ones ShieldsUP! was created to warn people about.

quiz.q: How did the worm get past corporate firewalls?
options: Telecommuters' infected laptops were plugged in at work
quiz.explain: Laptops were infected over the weekend, then plugged into the internal network on Monday, where machines had no personal firewalls.
